variants.title: Run the request loop
variants.context: A personalized response comes from a policy joining identity, consent, current context, evidence, generation, and measurement. The base answer stays the fallback, so missing or denied signals reduce personalization rather than failing the request.
variants.prompt: A learner asks a tutoring question. Put the personalization stages in order.

items.text: Apply the chosen adaptation path: a request prompt, retrieval, routing, or a learned adapter.
Apply the policy gate, admitting only signals that are relevant, consented, authorized, and safe for this task.
Load explicit preferences and fresh inferred claims with their source, purpose, confidence, and expiry.
Return the response, expose why adaptation happened, and propose bounded profile updates from the feedback.
Resolve the user or session, the tenant, the task, and the current authorization boundary.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what the generation provider is even allowed to see?
variants.explanation: The policy gate sits between loading claims and using them, so only authorized signals reach prompt assembly or retrieval.

variants.title: Run the request loop
variants.context: A personalized response comes from a policy joining identity, consent, current context, evidence, generation, and measurement. The base answer stays the fallback, so missing or denied signals reduce personalization rather than failing the request.
variants.prompt: The profile store is unavailable during a support request. Put the stages in order.

items.text: The policy gate admits only the current session context, since nothing else can be checked for consent.
The profile read fails, so no stored claims are available for this request.
The base answer is generated from request context alone, as a fallback rather than an error.
Identity, tenant, and task still resolve from the request itself.
The response is identified as non-personalized where that distinction matters to the user.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what the generation provider is even allowed to see?
variants.explanation: Missing profile storage degrades personalization to the base answer instead of failing the product.

variants.title: Run the request loop
variants.context: A personalized response comes from a policy joining identity, consent, current context, evidence, generation, and measurement. The base answer stays the fallback, so missing or denied signals reduce personalization rather than failing the request.
variants.prompt: A request would pull in a document that belongs to a different tenant. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Profile claims load with their consent version and the source permissions attached to each one.
The policy gate fails closed on the cross-tenant document before retrieval or prompt assembly begins.
The response records which signals were denied, so the decision can be explained later.
Identity resolution fixes the requesting user, their tenant, and the authorization boundary for this task.
Adaptation continues using only the claims and sources this tenant is actually permitted to use.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what the generation provider is even allowed to see?
variants.explanation: Cross-tenant requests fail closed before retrieval, because semantic similarity is never an authorization check.

variants.title: Promote a claim
variants.context: Feedback is a proposal, not a fact. Observe a bounded event, aggregate repeated evidence into a typed candidate claim, evaluate it against the generic baseline, then promote or discard it with correction and deletion paths intact.
variants.prompt: A learner keeps opening worked examples. Put the promotion steps in order.

items.text: Promote only a justified claim, tell the user where appropriate, and keep correction, rollback, and deletion paths.
Compare the candidate with the generic baseline and check quality, safety, privacy, and cohort effects.
Record a bounded event with the task, response variant, outcome, timestamp, and consent scope.
Aggregate the repeated evidence into a candidate claim with confidence, an expiry, and any counter-evidence.

variants.hint: One observation is evidence; a durable claim needs more than that.
variants.explanation: Observations become candidate claims, and only evaluation against the baseline can justify promoting one.

variants.title: Promote a claim
variants.context: Feedback is a proposal, not a fact. Observe a bounded event, aggregate repeated evidence into a typed candidate claim, evaluate it against the generic baseline, then promote or discard it with correction and deletion paths intact.
variants.prompt: A candidate claim that this user prefers shorter answers fails its evaluation. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Evaluation against the generic baseline shows lower task success for the same users.
They were aggregated into one candidate preference carrying a confidence score and an evidence window.
The candidate is discarded rather than activated, and the negative evidence is preserved.
The clicks that followed short answers were logged as bounded events, without copying unnecessary response content.

variants.hint: A click is ambiguous: it can mean concise or it can mean incomplete.
variants.explanation: Negative evidence is kept, because separating what a user saw from what a user preferred is what breaks the feedback loop.

variants.title: Promote a claim
variants.context: Feedback is a proposal, not a fact. Observe a bounded event, aggregate repeated evidence into a typed candidate claim, evaluate it against the generic baseline, then promote or discard it with correction and deletion paths intact.
variants.prompt: An old inferred preference may no longer hold after the learner changed roles. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The stale claim is decayed or retired, and the user keeps a direct way to correct it.
Reserved exploration traffic serves the generic variant, so the alternative can be observed at all.
Those observations are aggregated into counter-evidence against the existing claim.
The claim is retested against the baseline for the learner's current task and role.

variants.hint: A system that only serves the old preference can never learn it is wrong.
variants.explanation: Exploration traffic and claim decay are what stop personalization from reinforcing an out-of-date inference.

variants.title: Measure the delta
variants.context: A personalization release compares a generic baseline with a personalized candidate. The lesson's illustrative gate uses uplift in percentage points, policy overhead under 150 ms measured separately from generation, and a deletion drill that must cover every declared derived store.
variants.prompt: A release compares the same evaluation set on both arms. The generic baseline scores 61 percent task success and the personalized candidate scores 73 percent. What is the uplift?
variants.hint: Compare the two scores directly rather than as a ratio.
variants.explanation: 73 minus 61 is 12 percentage points of uplift over the same generic baseline, which is why every case needs both arms.

mistakes.feedback: That is the relative change; the gate reports the difference in percentage points.
That is the candidate score, not its delta over the baseline.

variants.title: Measure the delta
variants.context: A personalization release compares a generic baseline with a personalized candidate. The lesson's illustrative gate uses uplift in percentage points, policy overhead under 150 ms measured separately from generation, and a deletion drill that must cover every declared derived store.
variants.prompt: Policy overhead has a 150 ms budget. Claim loading takes 40 ms, the consent check takes 25 ms, and retrieval authorization takes 55 ms. How much headroom is left in the budget?
variants.hint: Add every policy stage before comparing with the budget.
variants.explanation: 40 plus 25 plus 55 is 120 ms of policy overhead, leaving 30 ms. Generation time is measured separately from this budget.

mistakes.feedback: That is the overhead already spent, not the headroom that remains.
That subtracts only one stage from the budget.

variants.title: Measure the delta
variants.context: A personalization release compares a generic baseline with a personalized candidate. The lesson's illustrative gate uses uplift in percentage points, policy overhead under 150 ms measured separately from generation, and a deletion drill that must cover every declared derived store.
variants.prompt: A team declares 8 derived stores that a deletion request must clear. The deletion drill confirms removal in 6 of them. What percentage did the drill confirm?
variants.hint: Divide what the drill proved by what the team declared.
variants.explanation: 6 of 8 declared stores is 75 percent, so a gate that requires every declared store to be confirmed does not pass.

mistakes.feedback: That is the release requirement, not what the drill actually confirmed.
That is the share still unconfirmed.

variants.title: Type the signal
variants.context: A profile holds small typed claims rather than a biography. Explicit preferences are user stated, session context is short lived, inferred preferences are probabilistic, and private knowledge stays access controlled at retrieval time.
variants.prompt: A team is defining its profile schema. Match each signal class to how it must be handled.

pairs.label: Explicit preference
pairs.detail: Keep the exact scope the user stated and offer an edit or reset control.

pairs.label: Session context
pairs.detail: Improve one request with the current task, device, or locale without becoming durable memory.

pairs.label: Inferred preference
pairs.detail: Store confidence, an evidence window, an expiry, and a way for the user to reject it.

pairs.label: Private knowledge
pairs.detail: Enforce tenant and document permissions at retrieval, since profile consent does not grant source access.

variants.hint: Ask where each signal came from and how long it should last.
variants.explanation: Typed claims can be traced and corrected, which an unstructured biography of the user cannot.

variants.title: Type the signal
variants.context: A profile holds small typed claims rather than a biography. Explicit preferences are user stated, session context is short lived, inferred preferences are probabilistic, and private knowledge stays access controlled at retrieval time.
variants.prompt: Match each observed signal to the class it belongs in.

pairs.label: The user selects Spanish in settings
pairs.detail: Explicit preference, kept at the stated scope with an edit and reset control.

pairs.label: The request arrives on a slow mobile connection
pairs.detail: Session context, useful for this response and not stored as memory.

pairs.label: The learner opened worked examples three weeks running
pairs.detail: Inferred preference, stored with confidence, expiry, and a rejection path.

pairs.label: The team handbook this user is entitled to read
pairs.detail: Private knowledge, authorized at retrieval by document permissions.

variants.hint: Ask where each signal came from and how long it should last.
variants.explanation: Classifying the signal first is what decides its retention, its consent requirement, and its correction path.

variants.title: Type the signal
variants.context: A profile holds small typed claims rather than a biography. Explicit preferences are user stated, session context is short lived, inferred preferences are probabilistic, and private knowledge stays access controlled at retrieval time.
variants.prompt: Match each field of a profile claim to what it records.

pairs.label: Value and purpose
pairs.detail: What may change in the response and which product task that change serves.

pairs.label: Provenance
pairs.detail: Whether the user stated it, the session supplied it, or behavior suggested it.

pairs.label: Confidence and freshness
pairs.detail: How certain the claim is and when it should expire or be reconfirmed.

pairs.label: Lifecycle
pairs.detail: Who may inspect, correct, export, or delete it, and which derived stores must follow.

variants.hint: Ask which field an auditor would read to answer a deletion request.
variants.explanation: A claim without provenance, expiry, and a lifecycle cannot be explained to the user or reliably removed.

variants.title: Climb the ladder
variants.context: Start with the least persistent mechanism. A request prompt is inspectable and cheap to change, retrieval suits private or changing knowledge, routing gives specialization by cohort, and a learned adapter is the hardest layer to version, evaluate, and delete.
variants.prompt: A user wants a warmer tone, and their stated preference changes every few weeks. Where should the team start?
options: Train a per-user adapter on their past conversations.
Insert the stated claim into the request prompt for this task.
Route these users to a separately fine-tuned model.
optionFeedback: An adapter makes a fast-changing preference slow to update and hard to delete.
Right: a stated preference that changes weekly is exactly what a small, inspectable prompt claim handles.
Routing to another model is a much heavier change than editing one claim.
variants.hint: Ask how often this behavior changes and how quickly it must be revocable.
variants.explanation: Escalate the adaptation layer only when measured failures justify a more persistent mechanism.

variants.title: Climb the ladder
variants.context: Start with the least persistent mechanism. A request prompt is inspectable and cheap to change, retrieval suits private or changing knowledge, routing gives specialization by cohort, and a learned adapter is the hardest layer to version, evaluate, and delete.
variants.prompt: An enterprise cohort needs a different tool path and prompt bundle for the same task. Which layer fits?
options: Model or expert routing selected by task and cohort.
One fine-tuned model maintained per customer account.
A longer prompt that spells out every cohort's rules.
optionFeedback: Right: routing gives specialization without maintaining one model per person or per account.
Per-account models multiply versioning, evaluation, rollback, and deletion work.
Packing every cohort's rules into one prompt spends context and blurs the behavior.
variants.hint: Ask how often this behavior changes and how quickly it must be revocable.
variants.explanation: Routing supplies cohort specialization at the capability layer, without a persistent per-user artifact.

variants.title: Climb the ladder
variants.context: Start with the least persistent mechanism. A request prompt is inspectable and cheap to change, retrieval suits private or changing knowledge, routing gives specialization by cohort, and a learned adapter is the hardest layer to version, evaluate, and delete.
variants.prompt: After two weeks of click data, a team proposes a per-user fine-tune. What should the reviewer ask first?
options: Whether the training run fits inside the current compute budget.
Whether the adapter raises average engagement over the last release.
Whether consented examples show a stable gap the cheaper layers missed.
optionFeedback: Cost is real, but it says nothing about whether this layer is needed at all.
Average engagement can rise while deletion, rollback, and cohort quality get worse.
Right: an adapter is justified only by a stable behavior gap that prompt, retrieval, and routing could not close.
variants.hint: Ask how often this behavior changes and how quickly it must be revocable.
variants.explanation: A learned adapter needs enough consented examples and a stable gap, because versioning and deletion get harder at that layer.
